options: Nothing: ill-formed, the deduction is ambiguous
questions.explanation: When a braced list has a single element whose type is a specialization of the class template being deduced, the initializer-list phase is skipped, so the copy deduction candidate `vector(vector<T>) -> vector<T>` wins with `T = int`. `v` is a copy of `other` with three elements. Wrapping was the result before P0702 fixed it for C++17, and it is what you get with two elements, `std::vector v{other, other}`.

`std::pair` has the deduction guide `pair(T1, T2) -> pair<T1, T2>`, which takes its parameters by value. Deducing a by-value parameter from an array argument decays it, so `T2` is `const char*` and `p` is `std::pair<int, const char*>`. An array type is tempting because the constructor taking `const T2&` would preserve it, but the guide is what decides the type here.

options: Ill-formed: `std::pair` needs two template arguments, and CTAD is all or nothing
Well-formed: `p` is `std::pair<int, int>`, and 2.0 is narrowed
questions.explanation: Class template argument deduction happens only when the template name appears with no argument list at all. Once `<int>` is written, the name refers to `std::pair<int>`, which is an invalid template-id because the second parameter has no default. There is no partial deduction; use `std::pair<int, double>`, `std::pair p{1, 2.0}`, or a factory function.

options: Nothing: `v` is ill-formed because iterators are not characters
questions.explanation: With braces, initializer-list constructors are tried first, so `std::vector(std::initializer_list<T>)` deduces `T = std::string::iterator`, and `v` holds the two iterators. The single-element copy rule does not apply because there are two elements. With parentheses there is no initializer-list phase, and the iterator-pair guide deduces `std::vector<char>` with five characters.

options: Well-formed: `T&&` is a forwarding reference, so `h` is `Holder<int&>`
Ill-formed: `T&&` names a class template parameter, so it is not a forwarding reference and cannot bind `i`
Well-formed: `h` is `Holder<int>`, initialized from a copy of `i`
Ill-formed: a class template cannot be deduced from a reference parameter
questions.explanation: The implicit guide is `template <class T> Holder(T&&) -> Holder<T>`, but [temp.deduct.call] excludes a class template parameter from being a forwarding reference during CTAD. So `T` deduces as `int` from the lvalue, the guide's parameter is `int&&`, and it cannot bind to `i`. Without this rule `Holder<int&>` would be deduced, which is the tempting answer and would usually not be what the class author meant. A user-defined guide with its own `template <class U> Holder(U&&)` parameter does forward.

options: Ill-formed: an explicit guide cannot be used in copy-initialization
questions.explanation: In copy-initialization that is not list-initialization, explicit candidates are not considered, so the guide is ignored for `b`. That leaves the implicit guide from `Box(T)`, which takes `T` by value and decays the array: `Box<const char*>`. For the direct-initialization of `a`, the guide and the constructor's implicit guide match equally well, and the tie goes to the guide, which is both user-defined and a non-template, so `a` is `Box<std::string>`. Only copy-list-initialization, `Box c = {"hi"};`, would be ill-formed, because there an explicit candidate is considered and then rejected.

questions.prompt: In C++20, which of these declarations are well-formed?
questions.code:
template <class T> struct Agg { T a; T b; };

Agg x{1, 2};     // #1
Agg y(1, 2);     // #2
Agg z{1, 2.0};   // #3
options: None: an aggregate needs a user-defined deduction guide
questions.explanation: C++20 adds an aggregate deduction candidate formed from the aggregate's element types and the initializer's elements, used for braced and for parenthesized aggregate initialization, so #1 and #2 deduce `Agg<int>`. In #3 the candidate is `template <class T> Agg(T, T)`, and deducing `T` from `int` and `double` conflicts, so deduction fails and #3 is ill-formed; no common type is computed. "None" is the C++17 answer, when aggregates needed explicit guides.

options: Ill-formed: a deduced class type cannot be the type of a non-static data member
Ill-formed: a default member initializer cannot use braces with CTAD, but `= {1, 2}` would work
questions.explanation: [dcl.type.class.deduct] allows a placeholder for a deduced class type only in an initializing declaration of a variable, a functional cast, a `new` expression, and the type of a non-type template parameter. A non-static data member is none of these, whatever form its default member initializer takes, so you must write `std::vector<int>`. A `static inline` data member is a variable, so CTAD would work there.
